lessons.title: Read The Shape Of A Dataset
lessons.hook: A pile of numbers means nothing until you know where they sit and how far they spread.

blocks.heading: One call, the whole shape of a dataset
blocks.body: When you get a new dataset, you want its shape before anything else: where the values sit, how spread out they are, and whether the data types match what you expect. Call .describe() on a DataFrame or Series and pandas hands you count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, the three quartiles, and the maximum in one table. The mean tells you the center; the standard deviation tells you how far values typically wander from it. Compare the mean to the median (the 50% row) to spot skew: when they differ a lot, a few extreme values are pulling the mean away from where most data actually sits.

blocks.code:
import pandas as pd

salaries = pd.Series([40, 42, 45, 47, 300])
print(round(salaries.mean(), 1))
print(salaries.median())
blocks.caption: Mean and median disagree because one salary pulls the mean up.

blocks.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "student": ["Ali", "Sara", "Omar", "Lina"],
    "score": [88, 92, 79, 95],
    "passed": [True, True, False, True],
})

print(round(df["score"].mean(), 1))
print(round(df["score"].std(), 1))
print(df.dtypes["passed"])

steps.say: One row per student keeps score and passed together, so every stat lines up with the right person.
Mean gives the center, but one wild score can drag it away from where most students cluster.
Standard deviation shows how far scores typically sit from that center, something the mean alone can't tell you.
Checking dtype confirms passed loaded as a boolean, not text, so later comparisons behave correctly.

blocks.caption: Full summary stats plus a dtype check, all in a few lines.

blocks.prompt: A gym logs five members' ages: 21, 22, 22, 23, 60. Predict exactly what this prints.
blocks.code:
import pandas as pd

ages = pd.Series([21, 22, 22, 23, 60])
print(round(ages.mean(), 1))
print(ages.median())
blocks.hint: Add all five ages and divide by 5 for the first line; sort them and read off the middle value for the second.
blocks.explain: The 60-year-old pulls the mean up to 29.6, well above everyone else's age, while the median stays at 22 because only the middle value counts.

blocks.prompt: Two classes both average 75 on a test. Class A has a standard deviation of 2; Class B has one of 18. Which statement is true?
options: Class A's scores cluster tightly near 75; Class B's scores vary widely around 75.
Class A and Class B have identical distributions since their means match.
Class B's students scored higher on average than Class A's.
Standard deviation only matters when the two means differ.
why: Correct: a small standard deviation means values cluster close to the mean.
Wrong: identical means say nothing about how spread out each group's scores are.
Wrong: a larger standard deviation says nothing about which mean is higher, and both means are 75 here.
Wrong: standard deviation measures spread whether or not two means happen to differ.
blocks.hint: Standard deviation measures distance from the mean, not the mean's value itself.
blocks.explain: Same mean, very different spread: Class A's scores barely move from 75, while Class B's swing widely above and below it.

blocks.prompt: Write `spread(values)` so it returns the standard deviation of a list of numbers, rounded to 1 decimal place, using pandas. For example, `spread([5, 5, 5, 5])` returns `0.0`.
blocks.hint: Wrap values in pd.Series(...), call .std() on it, then round the result to 1 decimal.
blocks.explain: pd.Series(values).std() computes the sample standard deviation directly; rounding to 1 decimal keeps the answer readable.

bullets: .describe() gives count, mean, std, quartiles, and max in one call.
Compare mean to median to catch outliers pulling the average away.
Standard deviation says how spread out values are around the mean.
blocks.remember: Mean plus median plus standard deviation together beat any single number alone.

blocks.say: Time to run these stats on a dataset of your own and see what the numbers actually say.

lessons.exitLine: Grab a real dataset next and let pandas show you what it is actually made of.
